metadata.file_name: 33. McJames et al. (2024). Little and often: Causal inference machine learning demonstrates the benefits of homework for improving achievement in mathematics and science.pdf
metadata.title: Little and often: Causal inference machine learning demonstrates the benefits of homework for improving achievement in mathematics and science

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 seventh cycle microdata and restricts the analysis to the Irish eighth-grade subset (n=4118). TIMSS employed a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design sampling complete classes within schools; the authors state that the resulting sampling weights were fully accounted for by appropriately weighting the analysis. The manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name nor any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it explicitly indicates complex survey weighting was applied to obtain nationally representative estimates. For data preparation, the authors also impute missing values (6% missing) using missRanger to retain the representative sample, and they aggregate homework frequency/duration categories to reduce sparsity before fitting the Bayesian Causal Forests model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 (seventh cycle) microdata and focused exclusively on the Irish eighth-grade subset (second year of secondary school). Homework frequency and duration were taken from the student questionnaire for mathematics and science; later analyses aggregated sparse categories (frequency: up to once/twice per week, three/four times per week, every day; duration: up to 15 min, 16–30 min, >30 min). Missing data (6%) were imputed with missRanger to avoid listwise deletion, and the model included a random intercept to account for the nested student-within-school structure.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Average treatment effects (ATEs) with 95% credible intervals; scaled effects reported as standard-deviation units. Key ATEs: Frequency every day vs up to once/twice per week: 7.51 points (1.63, 16.57), scaled 0.10 (0.02, 0.23). Frequency three/four times per week vs up to once/twice per week: 2.88 points (-3.61, 10.88), scaled 0.04 (-0.05, 0.15). Duration 16–30 min vs up to 15 min: -0.98 points (-3.85, 1.94), scaled -0.01 (-0.05, 0.03). Duration >30 min vs up to 15 min: 0.12 points (-3.37, 3.72), scaled 0.00 (-0.05, 0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Ireland) the study leveraged total instructional time, school emphasis on success, motivation and confidence, parents education level, and books at home to estimate causal effects of homework frequency and duration on mathematics achievement, finding that increasing homework frequency to every day produced a positive ATE of 7.51 points (95% credible interval 1.63–16.57) relative to up to once/twice per week. This indicates that policy and classroom practice should prioritize frequent (daily) short homework routines to improve mathematics achievement, while longer-duration homework beyond 15 minutes shows no clear causal benefit.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Average treatment effects (ATEs) with 95% credible intervals; scaled effects reported as standard-deviation units. Key ATEs: Frequency three/four times per week vs up to once/twice per week: 5.31 points (2.35, 8.25), scaled 0.07 (0.03, 0.10). Frequency every day vs up to once/twice per week: -1.94 points (-5.96, 2.28), scaled -0.02 (-0.07, 0.03). Duration 16–30 min vs up to 15 min: 1.80 points (-1.37, 5.32), scaled 0.02 (-0.02, 0.06). Duration >30 min vs up to 15 min: 3.27 points (-2.20, 9.30), scaled 0.04 (-0.03, 0.11).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Ireland) the study leveraged total instructional time, school emphasis on success, motivation and confidence, parents education level, and books at home to estimate causal effects of homework frequency and duration on science achievement, finding that the optimal homework frequency was three to four times per week with an ATE of 5.31 points (95% credible interval 2.35–8.25) relative to up to once/twice per week. This indicates that homework policy should be subject-specific—encouraging moderately frequent homework in science rather than daily homework—while evidence does not support longer-duration homework beyond 15 minutes as reliably beneficial.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderation results are presented visually (Fig. 4) as individual treatment effect variation by home resources and parental education; the paper reports no clear trend indicating similar predicted benefits across socioeconomic levels.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics and Science (Ireland) the study leveraged books at home, parents education level, school average SES, motivation and confidence, and total instructional time to assess whether socioeconomic advantage moderates the causal effect of homework frequency/duration. It found no clear trend that advantaged students benefit more than peers, indicating approximately similar predicted homework gains across socioeconomic groups. This indicates that, at least for Irish eighth graders in mathematics and science, well-designed homework frequency policies may improve achievement without widening socioeconomic achievement gaps, though unmeasured confounding and model assumptions remain limitations.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 seventh-cycle data for Ireland, restricting to 4118 eighth-grade students and using homework frequency and duration categories from the student questionnaire for both mathematics and science. Achievement is measured with TIMSS rotated booklets and five plausible values per subject; the authors pool across plausible values and report causal average treatment effects (ATEs) with 95% credible intervals from a multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests model (BCF) that estimates potential outcomes and conditional average treatment effects. Homework frequency shows clear subject-specific benefits: in mathematics, daily homework increases achievement by 7.51 points (1.63–16.57), while in science the best frequency is three to four times per week (5.31 points; 2.35–8.25), with daily homework not showing clear benefit. Homework duration beyond 15 minutes does not show clear causal gains in either subject. The study imputes 6% missing data using missRanger and applies TIMSS sampling weights, but causal interpretation still depends on BCF assumptions and the authors’ ability to control confounding.
